item.title: Melania Trump secures ceasefire in Russian-held Ukrainian city, White House says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
First lady Melania Trump (Finn Gomez/Getty Images) First lady Melania Trump has successfully negotiated a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine to allow humanitarian aid and civilian evacuations in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, revealed for the first time Friday on Newsmax's " National Report ." Appearing live in the Newsmax studio, Beckman disclosed that representatives of both countries had signed the agreement just hours before his appearance, marking a significant humanitarian breakthrough in the nearly five-year war. "Let me start by being very crystal clear: the first lady of the United States of America has successfully negotiated a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, localized in this region of Oleshky," Beckman told Newsmax. The ceasefire, scheduled to begin Oct. 29, will allow Ukrainian and Russian civilian representatives to enter Oleshky, about 5 miles behind the front lines, to identify residents needing assistance and coordinate evacuations, Beckman said. "It will bring humanitarian aid to the entire city, this includes medics, medicine, food, clean water," he said, noting the operation will include "an evacuation of the city of Oleshky as well." Newsmax has been granted exclusive television access to accompany a delegation of Russian and Ukrainian observers entering Oleshky on Oct. 29. Both Ukrainian and Russian officials agreed to allow Newsmax to document the humanitarian operation. Beckman emphasized the immediacy of the breakthrough, revealing that the agreement had only just been finalized. "As recently as this morning, I'm coming here, and the ink is still wet on the paper," he said. He said the agreement had been signed just hours before his Newsmax appearance. "So you're the first to know," Beckman said. Residents Facing Starvation Oleshky, located in southern Ukraine's Kherson region, had about 24,000 residents before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Fewer than 2,000 residents remain, primarily elderly civilians unable to escape, along with approximately 50 children. Conditions have deteriorated dramatically, with residents facing severe food shortages, limited electricity, no running water, and no heat. Roads around Oleshky are reportedly heavily mined and targeted by armed drones. One route connecting Oleshky with nearby Radensk has become known as the "Road of Death" because it is littered with destroyed vehicles. Beckman described an increasingly desperate humanitarian emergency. "They're eating weeds and grass," he told Newsmax, describing reports of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement released Friday, Melania Trump said her intervention was essential to prevent further suffering. "The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," the first lady said. "Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water." "It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible." Beckman revealed on Newsmax that the negotiations began after the first lady learned about Oleshky's humanitarian crisis during her Fostering the Future Together event held in conjunction with the United Nations General Assembly in September. Her earlier efforts to reunite children separated from their families during the war helped establish direct communication channels with Russian and Ukrainian leaders. The first lady has helped facilitate the reunification of 34 Ukrainian and Russian children with their families since the war began. "Both sides formally recognized her as an intermediary and in writing, and they gave her the power to negotiate this ceasefire," Beckman said. Beckman said the first lady spent more than a month negotiating with both governments to finalize the agreement. The first lady said representatives from both countries will visit residents in their homes, assess their needs, and arrange transportation for those wishing to leave. "Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination," Trump said. "I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine." Newsmax cameras will document the operation, providing independent visibility into the evacuation process and whether residents' wishes are respected. A Possible Step Toward Peace Although the agreement is limited to Oleshky and does not establish a broader ceasefire, Beckman expressed hope that it could lead to further diplomatic progress. "Indeed, in my opinion, this is the first step towards everlasting peace between these two nations," he said. Beckman said Ukrainian and Russian representatives were enthusiastic when signing the agreement, saying both countries' presidents had supported the first lady's efforts. Nevertheless, he cautioned against assuming the humanitarian breakthrough would immediately produce a comprehensive peace agreement. "My hope is that this ceasefire... creates a better peace within the region for Europe," Beckman said. For now, the immediate priority remains delivering desperately needed supplies and providing a safe passage out of Oleshky. The unprecedented arrangement puts Melania Trump at the center of a rare cooperative humanitarian effort between the warring nations Important: Download the free Newsmax App on your smartphone and get latest updates from Ukraine, Russia and our breaking news! item.title: 2 former FBI officials charged with lying to Congress about Hunter Biden laptop probe
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jeanine Pirro, U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia. (Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty ) WASHINGTON — Two former FBI officials who have come under withering criticism from allies of President Donald Trump have been charged with allegedly lying to Congress over the investigation into former President Joe Biden’s son Hunter Biden. A court docket shows that Nikki Floris, the former deputy assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence Division, and Bradley Benavides, another FBI official, were facing one count of the rarely-charged criminal offense which can be difficult to prosecute. Hunter Biden was investigated, charged and eventually convicted of gun and tax crimes, before his father pardoned him shortly leaving office. U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in a social media post that Floris and Benavides had surrendered Friday morning. She alleged that the duo lied about their roles in the Foreign Influence Task Force and “about their roles in the FBI’s Hunter Biden investigations.” Attorneys for Floris said in a statement that Floris was “a patriot” who “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years” and was charged so the administration could “push a false narrative for a shot at political points.” Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill on Oct. 22, 2019. (Susan Walsh / AP) Attorneys Margaret Donovan, Chris Mattei, Mary Dohrmann and Kyle R. Freeny said in a statement that the “DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.” An attorney for Benavides was not listed yet on the court docket. The case was brought through a criminal complaint. They have not yet been indicted by a federal grand jury in D.C., where grand jurors have been skeptical of cases brought during Trump’s second term. Earlier this year, federal grand jurors rejected an attempt to indict six sitting Democratic members of Congress over a video Trump criticized. Flores was the FBI’s security lead for the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has falsely claimed was stolen. A mob of Trump supporters violently broke into the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, in a failed effort to stop the certification of Democrat Joe Biden as president. They beat and bloodied law enforcement, shattered windows and broke through barriers. She joined the FBI as an intelligence analyst in 2005, working on the director’s daily briefing staff and helped produce intelligence documents. She was promoted in 2017 to the department’s counterterrorism division. Benavides is a former colleague of Floris who focused on election security, foreign influence and Chinese intelligence threats. Floris has also been under criticism from Republicans over emails in which she discussed intelligence work that were obtained by Congress and declassified in July by Trump. Republicans have alleged that FBI officials buried what they describe as a credible report on China’s efforts to influence the election in an effort to protect then-FBI Director Christopher Wray. Intelligence officials and her legal team have said the pullback was a standard administrative move for a report that may have been unverified or had flawed intelligence. item.title: Trump says he ordered lawsuit to potentially block certification of Alaska Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump on Friday said he told his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president's party is struggling. “I'm the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida. The lawsuit, filed late Thursday, centers on one of the president's longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan, who Republicans fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what's likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state's former congresswoman. The second Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg , has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate. The lawsuit by the Republican president's Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. “The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections. The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set. The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state's Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused. Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people. The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice's intervention. “We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course,” campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. “Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska.” Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses,” said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. In a statement on Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska's election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan's campaign was an attempt to “mislead” voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska's Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot. "The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters,” the department's statement said. The Department of Justice has increasingly been used to bolster the Republican president's political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump's party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the 2020 White House race to Democrat Joe Biden. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. “It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed. The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department. Constitution gives states the power to run elections Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lose the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. “The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” Muller said. “The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.” The U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards set by Congress. That division of power has frustrated Trump, who repeatedly has tried to seize control of election procedures through executive orders that courts have blocked . The final step for a state election is formally certifying the winner, the act that the administration's lawsuit seeks to prevent, it requests, “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan." The process in Alaska is complicated by the state's ranked choice voting system, which Trump opposes, and many expect it to take weeks before a winner is known. Also on the state's ballot is an initiative to repeal that system. Trump has stepped up complaints about a ballot with dueling Sullivans Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot, making reference to it during a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week where he called it “CHEATING.” “We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” the president wrote on Wednesday. Clogging a ballot with third party candidates to siphon off votes from the other major party is a long-standing tactic in the country's two-party system. Republicans have been linked to an effort to persuade Ohio voters to support a socialist in that state's Senate race, which could help Republican Sen. Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. ___ Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington, DC contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-administration-sues-block-alaska-144654098.html

item.title: Elon Musk is preparing for a Democratic Congress and warns he'll fight back
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Elon Musk has adopted a war posture in response to looming threats of congressional investigations: If Democrats win control of Congress in next month’s midterm elections, Musk has signaled he is bracing for a fight. “Live by the sword, die by the sword,” he said Wednesday in a post on X, responding to a Politico report that cited Democratic lawmakers seeking to investigate him. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets,” said Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX. Musk’s battle-ready stance comes as a host of Democrats have said they are eager to wield the power of their office to investigate the world’s richest person should they win either chamber in the midterms. As Republicans’ election prospects have soured, lawmakers are building momentum for probes looking into the tech mogul, his companies or the work of the U.S. DOGE Service, which Musk oversaw and which was instrumental in dismantling the U.S. Agency for International Development. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (Connecticut), the ranking Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, said in an interview Thursday that he would investigate Musk and DOGE if Democrats win. Blumenthal led inquiries relating to the cost-cutting group but was in the minority and did not have subpoena power, which could be used to compel the attendance of witnesses, as well as the production of documents and records. “The American people have a right to know the cost, the consequences and the chaos resulting from DOGE and … what he may be concealing,” Blumenthal said. “There is a web of potential corruption here that needs to be explored.” He dismissed Musk’s threats of retaliation, expressing surprise at his strong reaction. “He should have nothing to hide,” said Blumenthal, adding that he would expect a Democratic chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee to support efforts to investigate Musk. Musk did not respond to requests for comment. Diverging from many of his corporate peers, Musk has consistently countered threats with force. He has contested lawsuits, picked fights with powerful government officials and at times taken drastic action over business disputes, including changing his state of residence - and the locations of his businesses - from California to Texas. But Musk has also acknowledged his own vulnerability in an unfavorable political environment, joking in 2024 about the prospect of going to prison if President Donald Trump was not elected to a second term. Musk has also poured his resources into midterm races, eclipsing his donations toward Trump’s election in 2024. He is the largest individual donor in the 2026 midterm elections, putting more than $350 million toward efforts to elect Republicans. Musk and others who carried out DOGE’s agenda face a potential slew of subpoenas, investigations and hearings after the midterms, in which Democrats are heavily favored. Several other Democratic members of Congress have also raised the prospect of exploring Musk’s business or political ventures in recent days. Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Virginia), a member of the House Oversight Committee, tagged Musk in a post on X. “I’d just like you to explain to Congress and the American people why DOGE failed so miserably and why you then lied about the savings,” he wrote. “Will you commit to testifying under oath to explain?” Disputed legacy As an influential adviser to President Donald Trump last year, Musk oversaw the sweeping and at times chaotic U.S. DOGE Service campaign to cut costs at government agencies. Staffed largely with young tech workers new to government service who were chosen by Musk and his circle, DOGE eliminated the jobs of hundreds of thousands of federal workers and accessed sensitive data on hundreds of millions of Americans. Musk said that he aimed to cut $2 trillion in federal spending with DOGE, which ultimately claimed $215 billion in estimated savings. A Government Accountability Office audit found that the group consistently overstated its savings. DOGE took credit for lease cancellations set into motion before it existed, for example, and claimed savings from contracts that continued to exist. Musk has at times issued threats of retribution on X, the platform he bought in 2022 when it was named Twitter and later folded into his rocket company SpaceX. “There is a large graveyard filled with my enemies,” he wrote in a 2023 post. “I do not wish to add to it, but will if given no choice. Those who pick fights with me do so at their own peril, but maybe this is their lucky day.” The entrepreneur mused about his fate if Democrats took power in a 2024 interview with Tucker Carlson. “If he loses, I’m f---ed,” Musk said, going on to joke: “How long do you think my prison sentence is going to be?” “There may be some vengeance on me” if Trump doesn’t retake the White House, Musk said in the interview, which took place before the election. Should Democrats regain control of Congress this time, they will face pressure from some voters and activist groups to move on Musk. Activist group Investigate DOGE has channeled the spirit of the Tesla Takedown movement, which staged anti-Musk demonstrations outside Tesla showrooms, calling for Musk and DOGE alumni to face congressional scrutiny. Activists are asking, “‘How do we make sure Elon gets held accountable if Democrats take congress again?’” said Evan Sutton, a spokesman for the group. “Congress needs to get in there. They need to get their hands dirty. The American people need to know what happened.” Some former DOGE staffers are already taking precautions in the event of a Democratic-controlled Congress, seeking to insulate themselves from the potential outcomes of ethics probes by attempting to button up their post-DOGE business dealings. Though the midterms are still more than a week away, Musk continues to signal he’s readying a counteroffensive. Responding to a video of the tech journalist Kara Swisher noting that if Democrats take power, he “knows what’s coming,” Musk had a simple reply: “Message received.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/23/musk-says-he-will-fight-back-if-congressional-democrats-investigate-doge/

item.title: Kushner pushes back on report involving phone, spies, transfer
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jared Kushner is pushing back on a report involving a hacked iPhone, international spies and billion-dollar transfers from foreign governments. An upcoming book by journalist Matthew Cole claims Kushner, who is President Trump's son-in-law, had access to more than $2 billion in "slush money funds" from Middle Eastern leaders in an attempt to influence U.S. foreign policy. An excerpt of the book released Thursday details allegations encompassing Kushner's time as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration, which included a lead role in U.S. policy in the Middle East. Kushner had a major hand in negotiating key foreign policy deals that involved Israel, the Gulf states, China and Russia during that period. Kushner and his legal team released fiery statements Thursday night categorically denying all accusations against him. Kushner said , "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." His attorney called them "false and defamatory" and said they intend to pursue legal action against those responsible, but did not specify whom. The new book, "Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East," alleges Kushner had access to billions of dollars in undisclosed foreign bank accounts intended to pay for "influence within the U.S. government." An excerpt from the book that was published in "Vanity Fair," but not independently verified by CBS News, says Dutch intelligence agents learned the Russians had hacked Kushner's iPhone in 2017 after flipping a Russian spy and subsequently gained access to Kushner's phone as well. According to the report, "when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner's screen as he used it." At the time, Kushner served as a senior White House adviser to President Trump, including on Middle Eastern diplomacy. The report alleges Dutch spies witnessed him log into a United Arab Emirates account that had allegedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, and claims the leaders of Saudi Arabia and the UAE put at least $2 billion into multiple bank accounts linked to Kushner, including an account with Israel's Central Bank. According to the book excerpt, the owners and managers of the accounts were often disguised as official government entities or charities, but the funds were actually intended for "off-the-books diplomatic objectives" such as striking a deal to end the Israeli-Palesteinian conflict. The report also claims Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put roughly $1 billion into at least one account for Kushner, citing a "person with knowledge of the money" saying "its allocation was for Kushner's personal benefit." Kushner forcefully denied the accusations leveled in the "Vanity Fair" excerpt, writing in part, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." "We denied every claim on the record, yet the author provided not a single shred of verifiable evidence to substantiate them," he said. "No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said. CBS News reached out to the White House, which referred us to a statement from Steven Cheung, who is assistant to the president and White House director of communications. Cheung said the "bull**** Vanity Fair article comes from a book that is complete fiction, and was fabricated from the warped mind of failed spy thriller writer." "He presents no evidence or even a shred of documentation. Just mysterious words from unnamed sources," Cheung said on X. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jared-kushner-pushes-back-report-hacked-phone-spies-transfer/

item.title: President Trump unveils renovated Reflecting Pool with anti-vandal cameras
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump said Friday that the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is continuing to fill with water, declaring that the landmark is “looking really good” and will be protected by anti-vandalism cameras. The pool has become a recurring point of attention since Trump ordered it resurfaced in “American flag blue” ahead of the nation’s 250th anniversary celebrations. The project has faced rising costs, algae issues, and damage to its freshly installed lining. In a message posted to Truth Social in the early hours of Friday morning, Trump said the Reflecting Pool was 85 percent full, “and looking really good!” Trump added: “It hasn’t worked properly since 1922, but will now. We have cameras set up to stop any potential Vandalism, including the grassed areas, which were destroyed by chemical poisoning with a large, and very inappropriate, phrase. The grass was completely replaced!” The president also included in his post an image the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall, with the Lincoln Memorial centered in the distance. “President Trump promised to make D.C. safe and beautiful, and he’s delivering. For years, the Reflecting Pool sat neglected, plagued with algae, and leaking millions of gallons of water. Fixing it was common sense,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a statement provided to Newsweek on Friday. “It’s another example of President Trump restoring our nation’s capital for the American people.” However, people visiting the area on Friday had conflicting opinions about the Reflecting Pool when interviewed by Newsweek . One woman said she had not heard about the vandalism or debacle surrounding the pool this year but thought it looked “pretty.” Another woman told Newsweek she thought it “still looks like dirty water,” although she said she could see the reflection of the Washington Monument within it. A third woman told Newsweek she didn’t think the pool was reflective. “I used to live here years ago, and I would run around the mall all the time and you would be able to see a perfect reflection, and you can only see the base now so no it’s not,” she said. “It’s a little underwhelming, to be honest. It used to look much better to me, but I don’t really know what they’ve done or what they haven’t done or what’s been changed, so just, I’ve seen it on the news,” she added. “It was a big thing, and now being here, it just doesn’t look like it used to. It looks too dark, honestly.” Trump shared an image of the Reflecting Pool on the Truth Social platform on Friday. Cases Dropped Trump earlier this week threatened any potential vandals with jail time, reviving a dispute over cause of damage to the pool’s lining. A judge dismissed a case against former Olympian canoeist David Hearn this month, and federal prosecutors previously moved to dismiss the case after records suggested that a flawed installation, rather than vandalism, were to blame for the damage. Doug Buchanan, director of media and public relations for DC Courts, told Newsweek previously that he believed “there were three or four additional [vandalism] cases filed–but dismissed by the USAO/DC [U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia] before the cases made it to court.” Trump also alleged this week that grass near the pool had been “scarred by poison” with the numbers “86 47” , and said the turf had since been replaced. Algae, Peeling and Vandalism Claims Trump announced renovations in April , ahead of celebrations marking the 250th anniversary of American independence. The project involved resurfacing the bottom of the pool with a blue coating Trump described as “American flag blue.” NBC News reported that Trump initially estimated the work would cost between $1.5 million and $2 million and take one to two weeks, but that its cost subsequently rose to around $16 million. Problems emerged shortly after the pool was refilled . Its water turned green amid an algae bloom, while sections of the newly installed coating began to peel. Footage published by Newsweek in June showed the water changing color soon after the refurbishment, despite the pool’s new blue finish. A further contract was later awarded for renovation and maintenance work intended to tackle the algae, Newsweek reported previously . Trump has repeatedly attributed damage to vandals . Federal prosecutors said in a motion to dismiss Hearn’s case that records obtained from the Interior Department documented repeated failures of the lining during its installation and extensive peeling across the pool. The filing also pointed to pressure to complete the project before July 4. The Reflecting Pool has undergone major work before. A two-year reconstruction completed in 2012 addressed longstanding sinking and leakage, adding more than 2,000 supporting pilings and a circulation system drawing water from the nearby Tidal Basin, according to Histories of the National Mall. item.title: Ramaswamy defends attack ad featuring candidate's estranged mother
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy on Friday defended his campaign's ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton in the closely watched race for Ohio governor. Speaking at a campaign stop in northeast Ohio, he said the advertisement, which features Acton's mother calling her “a liar,” had nothing to do with childhood abuse. “The irony is they’re lying about an ad that is about lying,” Ramaswamy said. “They’re changing the subject because they don’t want to answer for their own failures." The advertisement features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, criticizing her and insinuating she has mental health issues. Arthur lost custody of her children after her husband, the children's stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton. Acton is Ohio’s former public health director and has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. She has condemned Ramaswamy for the ad. “I won’t normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I’m complaining about.” she told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio. A message seeking comment was sent Friday to her campaign The ad has stirred significant reaction , including from President Donald Trump, who said it was like “hitting pay dirt.” At a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday, Trump told the crowd Ramaswamy called him to ask for advice. “You’ve got to ride with it,” Trump recalled telling Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and former presidential candidate. Trump expressed jealousy that he didn’t have such a strong ad to run during his own campaigns. Other Republicans have been critical. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine criticized Ramaswamy and said the ad should be taken down. “It’s wrong to run this ad,” DeWine said Thursday. According to police and court documents obtained by The Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton’s biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty. He was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. He has since died. item.title: Minnesota officials say U.S. government stopped sharing evidence on fatal ICE shootings
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A card with images depicting Alex Pretti and Renee Good is placed at a makeshift memorial in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on 28 January 2026. Photograph: Seth Herald/Reuters The federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers during a violent anti-immigration, anti-protest crackdown in the state earlier this year, state officials said in recent court filings. Minnesota officials sued the Trump administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings. The family of Good, 37, earlier this month sued over her death when she was shot by a federal officer with Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) as she drove her car away during a protest in January. Pretti, also 37 , was shot dead in the street by a border patrol agent as he went to the assistance of a fellow protester on the icy city streets during fierce demonstrations against the crackdown. Both Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and ICE are under the umbrella of the Department of Homeland Security. The shootings of the two protesters, both US citizens, was a turning point in the government’s approach after weeks of violent action by ranks of militarized, masked federal immigration enforcement in Minneapolis, which local leaders called a siege , after months of similar mass operations in major cities. Related: Minneapolis leaders call the ICE surge a ‘siege’. My reporting from there concurs There were immediate disputes over the investigations into Good’s and later Pretti’s killings between state and federal authorities. The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don’t have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don’t trust the federal government to investigate itself. The state is still seeking the cellphones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews. State prosecutors announced in July that the federal government had begun turning over evidence in the cases, including police body-camera video and hard drives containing statements. The Hennepin county attorney, Mary Moriarty, said at the time that the state expected to receive “all the evidence”. But Minnesota investigators said in October court filings that the transfer of evidence stopped soon after the July announcement. Moriarty said the US attorney’s office for Minnesota, the state outpost of federal prosecutors, told her on 10 September that evidence sharing would be on pause indefinitely “in light of challenges with DC”, according to the documents, referring to Washington and the federal authorities. State prosecutors have again asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing they “have identified no legal authority or rational basis justifying their obstruction of state criminal investigations”. In a reply filed on Tuesday, attorneys for the US justice department argued it was within their discretion to decline to share information with state authorities. Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota bureau of criminal apprehension, said in a legal declaration that federal authorities still have Good’s clothing, the cellphone of the officer who killed her and interview recordings that state authorities have never been able to view. Bystanders captured footage of the shooting death of Good in her car and Pretti on the street , in each case contradicting key parts of what the administration said prompted the killings. No criminal charges have been filed. Evans said the federal government also has not shared a recorded statement from an officer who shot Pretti, the firearms used by the officers, their phones, projectiles and casings. The Associated Press contributed reporting This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/minnesota-officials-us-government-stopped-124647149.html

item.title: Meghan Markle says she was 'deeply distressed' by allegations against her father
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said she is "deeply distressed" by the news that her father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation over claims he possessed images containing child sexual abuse in his home. The images were reportedly found in his home in the Philippines after he returned to the U.S. in May, Philippine officials said. Thomas Markle denied the allegations, calling them "sick lies" and "the worst thing anyone could accuse me of." In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan Markle said that she is "deeply distressed" by the news, and that she was first made aware of the claims by the Met Police in 2018. "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan's statement said. "In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated. "I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. "I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families. "Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children." The allegations, reported by Mail Online , said Thomas Markle is under investigation after being reported by his son, Thomas Markle Jr. In a statement to Mail Online , the elder Markle said: "I'm shocked, I'm hurt and I'm very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I'm being accused of. It's the worst thing anyone could accuse me of. He added: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick. I have no idea why Tom [Markle] is trying to destroy me with these lies." Yahoo has contacted the Met Office and authorities in the U.S. and the Philippines for comment. This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/article/meghan-markle-deeply-distressed-as-father-thomas-is-investigated-over-alleged-child-sexual-abuse-material-120023185.html
